https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.overview_of_custom_object_relationships.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Due to the complexity of the Universal Containers sandbox release schedule and requirements, it is advised that change sets are used as often as possible to migrate from one environment to another. Which three common items can an app builder move when using a change set? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Web-to-Lead
optionC: Custom object
explanation:
Custom object, Apex class and Custom field are the three items a change set can move. All three are supported change-set components.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Web-to-Lead) — the Web-to-Lead setup is not a deployable component.
Option B (Standard fields) — standard fields are not deployed through change sets (only certain standard picklist values are).
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.changesets_about_components.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: The Service Manager provided the app builder with color code requirements for case age on open cases: New cases populate a green circle, day-old cases populate a yellow circle, three-day-old cases populate a red circle. How should an app builder implement this requirement?
optionA: Formula Field (image)
optionC: Custom Button
explanation:
A formula field returning an image is how the app builder implements it. A formula field that returns IMAGE() is the no-code way to put a coloured indicator on a record page, a list view or a report, and Salesforce documents this exact requirement as a worked sample: "Color Squares for Case Age" displays a 30 x 30 pixel red, yellow or green image depending on the value of a Case Age field.
Use nested IF() rather than CASE() when the trigger is an age range. CASE() checks an expression for equality against a list of values and returns the matching result, so it switches cleanly on a picklist such as Priority but cannot express "three days old or more". The documented age formula is IF(Case_Age__c > 20, IMAGE(red), IF(Case_Age__c > 10, IMAGE(yellow), IMAGE(green))), with IMAGE() taking a URL, alternate text, and optional height and width.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Quick Action) — something a user clicks, not a value that renders on every row of a list view.
Option C (Custom Button) — the same; a control, not an indicator.
Option D (Lightning Web Component) — custom development for something a formula field already does declaratively.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.useful_advanced_formulas_image_links.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.customize_functions_image.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.customize_functions_case.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Key A stands; the reasoning was rewritten on a factual point. The original prescribed IMAGE() with CASE() over case age, but CASE is documented as an equality check - "Checks a given expression against a series of values. If the expression is equal to a value, returns the corresponding result" - so it cannot express an age threshold. Salesforce's own sample for precisely this requirement, "Color Squares for Case Age", uses nested IF(). The same article's traffic-light sample confirms the wider claim that image formula fields are meant for list views and reports.

question: Cloud Kicks wants to efficiently increase the company's adoption of Salesforce while simultaneously moving away from their reliance on spreadsheets. An app builder is given a spreadsheet that needs to be added to Salesforce. The object with fields needs to be created and the data inserted simultaneously. Which tool should be used?
optionA: Import Wizard
optionC: Data Loader
explanation:
Lightning Object Creator is the tool. It takes a spreadsheet, Google Sheet or CSV, creates a new custom object with fields mapped from the columns, and imports the rows in a single guided flow.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Import Wizard) — loads data only into existing objects.
Option C (Data Loader) — the same; it creates no object.
Option D (Schema Builder) — creates objects and fields but imports no data.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.dev_objectcreate_task_lex_from_spreadsheet.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.faq_data_import_wizard_what_kind_objects.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: The marketing director is concerned that too many car parts were given away for free last year. Which functionality should be used to ensure all free parts receive the marketing director's sign-off?
optionA: Stack post
optionC: Automated email message
explanation:
An Approval process is the functionality. It formalises the sign-off requirement: when a record meets the entry criteria — Price = 0 or Discount = 100%, say — it must be submitted for approval, and the marketing director's approval is required before the record proceeds.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Stack post) — not a Salesforce feature.
Option B (Chatter approval) — a way to respond to an approval request from the feed, not the mechanism that requires the sign-off in the first place.
Option C (Automated email message) — notifies; it records no decision and blocks nothing.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.what_are_approvals.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.approvals_automated_actions.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers wants to display the real-time stock price for each account on the Account record page. How should an app builder implement this request?
optionA: Add a dynamic report to the page layout.
optionC: Install a solution from the AppExchange.
optionD: Build a flow that uses API calls.
explanation:
Installing a solution from the AppExchange is how an app builder implements it. Displaying a live stock price means calling an external financial API and rendering the result on the Account record page, and for an app builder the documented low-effort path is to install a prebuilt solution: browse or search AppExchange, click Get It Now, choose production or sandbox, install the package, then place the component it ships onto the Account record page in Lightning App Builder. The integration, the credential handling and the component are all work someone else has already done.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a dynamic report on the page layout) — reports run over Salesforce data; no report can reach an external price feed.
Option B (a Lightning Web Component) — custom development for a problem the marketplace already solves.
Option D (a flow using API calls) — the closest rival and no longer impossible: Flow's HTTP Callout connects a flow to an external API without code. But it is a build rather than a buy — it needs a named credential, an external service registration and familiarity with the provider's API contract, and the flow still has to be surfaced through a screen or a component before anything appears on the record page.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.distribution_installing_packages.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_http_callout.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Key C stands, but the explanation was rewritten because it left the strongest distractor unaddressed. Flow HTTP Callout is real and documented - "Use HTTP Callout to connect flows to external APIs without coding, eliminating the need for developers or middleware tools" - so option D is technically feasible today and the item turns on build-versus-buy for an app builder, not on D being impossible. Flagging this as a judgment item rather than a documented one: no Salesforce article says to use AppExchange for a stock price, and a reviewer who weighs the build-versus-buy reading differently could defend D.

question: Universal Containers has several new fields they've requested for the Opportunity Product object. What should an app builder be able to configure using a formula field?
optionA: A hyperlink to the parent Account of the parent Opportunity.
optionB: A Rich Text Area field that uses HTML to bold certain characters.
optionC: A combination of the Opportunity's Name and a Description field.
optionD: A mix of functions and concatenation of 10 Account fields and 10 Opportunity fields.
explanation:
A hyperlink to the parent Account of the parent Opportunity is what a formula field can configure. From Opportunity Product, formulas can traverse to the parent Opportunity and then to the parent Account, and the HYPERLINK() function can build a clickable URL to that grandparent Account record.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a Rich Text Area with HTML bolding) — formula fields cannot output rich text or HTML formatting.
Option C (Opportunity Name concatenated with a Description) — Description is a long text area, and long text area fields cannot be referenced in formulas.
Option D (functions over 10 Account and 10 Opportunity fields) — would likely exceed the compiled-formula size limit.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.fields_creating_cross_object_notes.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.formula_using_date_datetime.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: AW Computing uses a private sharing model for opportunities. Whenever an opportunity with a type of Service Agreement is created, all users in the Service Manager role should be able to view the opportunity. Which tool should AW Computing use to accomplish this?
optionA: Owner-based sharing rules
optionC: Apex sharing rules
explanation:
Criteria-based sharing rules are the tool. They grant access based on field values on the record itself — Type = Service Agreement — regardless of who owns it, which is exactly what is needed here.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (owner-based sharing rules) — share based on who owns the record, not on its content.
Option C (Apex sharing) — code for a case a declarative rule already covers.
Option D (manual sharing) — one record at a time, by hand; it cannot fire automatically on creation.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.managing_the_sharing_model.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers uses a custom picklist field Account Region on the Account record. They want this region to be reflected on all related Contact records and stay in sync if the value of this field changes on the Account. How should an app builder meet this requirement?
optionA: Create a picklist field 'Account Region' on Contact and a workflow rule to update it when the Account field changes.
optionB: Create a formula field on Contact set to ISPICKVAL(Account.Account_Region__c).
optionC: Create a formula field on Contact set to TEXT(Account.Account_Region__c).
optionD: Create a text field 'Account Region' on Contact and a workflow rule to update it when the Account field changes.
explanation:
A formula field on Contact set to TEXT(Account.Account_Region__c) is how to meet it. A cross-object formula returns the current picklist text from the parent Account and stays in sync automatically, with no automation required.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a Contact picklist synced by workflow) — a second copy that has to be kept in sync by automation, and workflow is past end of support.
Option B (ISPICKVAL(Account.Account_Region__c)) — ISPICKVAL returns a Boolean and takes two arguments; the wrong function and the wrong return type.
Option D (a Contact text field synced by workflow) — the same duplicated-copy problem as A.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.tips_for_using_picklist_formula_fields.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.customize_functions_text.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Northern Trail Outfitters uses a custom object to track travel requests. Rangers want to have automatic posts on a record whenever a travel request has been approved. Which feature should be used to accomplish this?
optionA: Auto-response rule
optionC: Feed tracking
explanation:
Feed tracking is the feature. Enabling Feed Tracking on the object and its Status field causes Chatter to post in the record's feed automatically when the tracked value changes — including "Status changed to Approved" — without any custom automation.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (auto-response rule) — sends email replies to leads and cases; it posts nothing to a feed.
Option B (workflow rule) — cannot post to Chatter, and is past end of support.
Option D (feed quick action) — lets a user post manually; the requirement is an automatic post.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.collab_feed_tracking.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: How should an app builder configure access to a Contact's Twitter profile for Salesforce mobile app users?
optionA: Add a formula field to the Contact page layout.
optionB: Add an AppExchange Lightning component to the mobile app.
optionC: Add the Twitter component to mobile-view Lightning pages.
optionD: Add a Twitter quick action to the mobile navigation.
explanation:
Adding the Twitter component to the mobile-view Lightning pages is how to configure it. Salesforce includes a standard Twitter Lightning component that can be added to record pages — with a Phone form factor in Lightning App Builder — to surface a Contact's Twitter profile and recent tweets in the mobile app.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a formula field on the page layout) — could hold a link, but it is not the Twitter profile integration.
Option B (an AppExchange component) — unnecessary; the component is standard.
Option D (a Twitter quick action in the navigation) — no such quick action exists.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.lightning_page_components.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers assigns system access via permission sets and permission set groups to ensure each user has proper access. One department with varying levels of support staff has five consistent permission sets they require in order to complete their duties. Some higher-level staff have additional permission sets that are only required for them. How should an app builder recommend assigning permission sets to users?
optionA: Use the Manage Assignments button to assign a permission set group and additional individual permission sets to each user.
optionB: Use the Manage Assignments button to assign each user with the same set of permission set groups and permission sets.
optionC: Use the Data Import Wizard to mass update the desired users with their full list of permission sets and permission set groups.
optionD: Use Data Loader to mass update the desired users with their full list of permission sets and permission set groups.
explanation:
Using the Manage Assignments button to assign a permission set group plus additional individual permission sets to each user is the recommendation. Bundle the five common permission sets into a permission set group and assign it to everyone in the department, then assign the additional individual permission sets to higher-level staff on top — the least maintenance, and the intended use of permission set groups.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (the same groups and sets for every user) — gives the support staff permissions only the higher-level staff need.
Option C (Data Import Wizard) — cannot load permission set assignments.
Option D (Data Loader) — can load PermissionSetAssignment records, but it is a bulk mechanism, not a recommendation for how to structure the assignments.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.perm_set_groups.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.faq_data_import_wizard_what_kind_objects.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: The services manager wants to make sure the team enters Case priority consistently. What feature can an app builder use to accomplish this?
optionA: Path
optionC: Next Best Action
explanation:
Path is the feature built for this. Salesforce describes it as a way to "boost productivity and help reps gather complete data", and at each step of a path you can highlight key fields and write customised guidance for success. Case is one of the supported objects, so a Case path built on the status picklist can surface Priority as a key field at every step, with guidance telling reps how to set it.
Path guides, it does not enforce. The documented limitation is explicit: you can't use the page layout to require different fields in different steps. If Priority has to be mandatory at a particular step, pair the path with a validation rule written against that path step.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Flow) — automates work behind the scenes rather than coaching the user at the point of entry.
Option C (Next Best Action) — surfaces recommended offers and actions, not field-entry guidance.
Option D (In-App Guidance) — delivers floating prompts and walkthroughs for feature adoption; not tied to the fields of the record being edited.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.path_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.path_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Key A stands; the explanation carried a factual error. It said Path key fields can be "required to fill out". Considerations and Guidelines for Creating Paths says the opposite: "You can't use the page layout to require different fields in different steps. However, you can set up validation rules based on a path step." Path highlights and guides; enforcement comes from a validation rule keyed to the step. The rest of the reasoning held - Guide Users with Path lists Cases among the supported objects and frames the feature as helping reps gather complete data, which is what the services manager asked for.

question: An app builder is creating a custom object called Testimonial__c and wants to connect Testimonial__c records with both the submitter's Contact record and Account record. If the Account is deleted, the Testimonial__c should also be deleted. If the Contact is deleted, but the Account remains, the Testimonial__c should remain. How should this be accomplished?
optionA: Make both the Contact and Account fields required on the Testimonial__c object and create lookup relationships from Testimonial__c to Contact and to Account.
optionB: Create a master-detail relationship from Testimonial__c to Account and a lookup relationship from Testimonial__c to Contact.
optionC: Make Testimonial__c a junction object between Account and Contact using master-detail relationships.
optionD: Create a lookup relationship from Testimonial__c to Account and a master-detail relationship from Testimonial__c to Contact.
explanation:
A master-detail relationship from Testimonial__c to Account and a lookup relationship from Testimonial__c to Contact is how to accomplish it. Master-detail to Account gives the cascade delete (deleting the Account deletes its testimonials), and the lookup to Contact lets the testimonial survive when the Contact is deleted.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (two required lookups) — a lookup does not cascade delete, so deleting the Account would leave the testimonials behind.
Option C (a junction object with two master-details) — deleting either parent would delete the testimonial, including the Contact.
Option D (lookup to Account, master-detail to Contact) — reversed: it would cascade-delete with the Contact and not with the Account.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.overview_of_custom_object_relationships.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Cloud Kicks has three types of customer support processes: Platinum, Diamond, and Bronze. The app builder created separate record types for each process on the Case object. The customer support team should be unable to create new cases with the Bronze record type. How should this requirement be met?
optionA: Update the organization-wide defaults to private for Case.
optionB: Update the support team profile to remove the Bronze record type assignment.
optionC: Create a permission set group for Case that includes Platinum and Diamond record types.
optionD: Make the record type hidden to support users; update sharing rules to private.
explanation:
Updating the support team profile to remove the Bronze record type assignment is how the requirement is met. Record type assignments are controlled at the profile (and permission set) level, and removing Bronze from the support team profile's assignments stops them from selecting it on new Case creation while keeping read access to existing Bronze records.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (OWD private for Case) — sharing governs who sees records, not which record types a user may create.
Option C (a permission set group including Platinum and Diamond) — adds record types; it does not remove Bronze if the profile still assigns it.
Option D (hide the record type and set sharing rules to private) — sharing rules only widen access, and hiding is what the profile assignment does; the option muddles two mechanisms.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_profiles_record_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.permissions_record_type_access.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.perm_sets_record_types_assign.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers' sales reps can modify fields on an opportunity until it is closed. The sales operations team has access to modify the Post-Close Follow-up Date and Post-Close Follow-up Comments fields after the opportunity is closed. After the opportunity is closed, the rest of the fields are read-only. How should these requirements be met?
optionA: Use record types with field sets and restrict editing fields using field-level security.
optionB: Use field-level security on page layouts to restrict editing fields.
optionC: Use field-level security on page layouts with record types to restrict editing fields.
optionD: Use field-level security to mark fields as read-only on the Sales profile.
explanation:
Field-level security on page layouts with record types is how these requirements are met. Use two record types, Open and Closed, each with its own page layout; on the Closed layout mark all fields except the two follow-up fields as read-only. Combined with profile-based record type assignment and field-level security, this delivers the differential editability described.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (record types with field sets) — field sets group fields for Visualforce and components; they do not control editability.
Option B (page-layout field security alone) — one layout cannot be read-only before close and editable after; the record type switch is what changes the layout.
Option D (read-only on the Sales profile via FLS) — profile FLS applies to every record regardless of stage, so reps could not edit open opportunities either.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.customize_layout.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_profiles_record_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A Service Coordinator (SC) for Ursa Major Solar (UMS) does a final review of work orders owned by a technician for a specific region before the records are submitted for an invoice. Before closing out the work order, the SC needs to modify data or remove attachments that were added by mistake. The SC also needs access to any other related records owned by the technician. What solution would provide the required access, given a private data model?
optionA: Give the SC a permission set with the Modify All Data system permission.
optionB: Put the SC in the role hierarchy above the technicians whose work orders they review.
optionC: Create a workflow rule that updates records owned by technicians in that region with the SC.
optionD: Change Work Order access on the SC's profile to Modify All.
explanation:
Putting the SC in the role hierarchy above the technicians whose work orders they review is the solution. Placing the SC above the technicians automatically grants read and edit access to all records owned by users below them, across all related objects — exactly the broad, regional supervisory access described — without resorting to org-wide Modify All Data.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Modify All Data) — org-wide access to every record of every object; far more than a regional review needs.
Option C (a workflow rule reassigning records to the SC) — changes ownership away from the technicians, and workflow is past end of support.
Option D (Modify All on Work Order in the profile) — covers work orders only; the SC also needs the technicians' other related records.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.managing_the_sharing_model.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: The case handling process at Universal Containers includes multiple steps including approvals, notifications, and field updates. To manage and evaluate all of these changes in a single save operation, an app builder wants to use Process Builder, and the advanced option to let the process evaluate a record multiple times has been selected. Which two options should the app builder avoid to prevent recursion? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: IF statements
optionB: Setting a criteria node to 'No criteria — just execute the actions'
optionC: Invocable processes
explanation:
Setting a criteria node to "No criteria — just execute the actions", and invocable processes, are the two options to avoid. With the option to let a process evaluate a record up to five times in a single save turned on, the risk is that an action re-triggers the same process. A criteria node with nothing to gate it fires again on each re-evaluation — the classic runaway — and invocable processes introduce mutual triggering, where one process calls another that updates a record and brings the first back into scope.
One important currency note about this whole item. Process Builder reached end of support on 31 December 2025. Existing processes continue to run and can still be edited, so the recursion behaviour described here is still real for orgs that have them, but nothing new should be built in Process Builder. In a record-triggered flow the equivalent discipline is entry conditions plus the option to run the flow only when specified changes are made.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (IF statements) — ordinary formula logic used inside criteria; a safeguard, not a hazard.
Option D (the ISCHANGED function) — narrows a criteria node to real transitions of a field, so it stops an action from re-firing when nothing relevant changed; the opposite of a recursion risk.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_build_data_update.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Key B,C stands, but this item is built entirely on a tool that reached end of support on 31 Dec 2025, and the explanation now says so. Per the established fact that this is retirement of support rather than removal of capability, the answer remains correct for orgs running existing processes, and the reasoning about ungated criteria nodes and mutually invocable processes is sound. Added the currency flag and named the record-triggered flow equivalent — entry conditions and running only when specified changes are made — so a learner takes away transferable guidance rather than only Process Builder mechanics. Flagged for the user: of the questions reviewed so far, this is the one most tied to a retired tool, and it may be worth rewriting around flows rather than keeping.

question: After utilizing the Lightning Object Creator to create a new object, its fields, and to insert all of the data, an app builder now needs to set up the Lightning record page. Which component should the app builder have on their Lightning record page to see all of the fields from the page layout?
optionA: Highlights Panel
optionC: Record Detail
explanation:
The Record Detail component is what shows all the fields from the page layout. The standard Record Detail Lightning component renders every section and field of the assigned page layout — the simplest way to expose the full layout on a Lightning record page.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Highlights Panel) — shows a handful of key fields and the action bar at the top of the page.
Option B (Recommendations) — surfaces Next Best Action recommendations; no fields.
Option D (Path) — renders the stage path for a picklist; it does not display the layout's fields.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.lightning_page_components.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: The Convert button on Leads should NOT appear until the Lead Status picklist is set to Qualified. What should an app builder suggest to meet these requirements?
optionA: Picklist dependency, page layouts, record types
optionB: Custom button, validation rule, record types
optionC: Process Builder field update, quick action, record type
optionD: Page layouts, record types, dynamic forms / dynamic actions
explanation:
Page layouts, record types, and dynamic forms / dynamic actions are what the app builder should suggest. Dynamic actions are what make an action's visibility depend on a field value: in Lightning App Builder you assign actions on the Lead record page's Highlights Panel instead of in the page layout editor, then click Add Filter to add visibility rules "based on the record field, device type, or other filters" — here, Lead Status equals Qualified. Below that value the Convert action simply is not rendered, and the standard convert flow is left intact.
Record types and page layouts are supporting cast rather than the mechanism. A layout is fixed for a given record type, so on its own it cannot show or hide Convert as a picklist value changes, and nothing moves a lead between record types when Status changes unless you build automation to do it. They earn their place only when a genuinely different kind of lead needs a different action set.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (picklist dependency, page layouts, record types) — confuses picklist dependencies, which control which values are offered in a dependent picklist, with action visibility.
Option B (custom button, validation rule, record types) — works, but replaces the standard Convert button with a custom one, which is more to build and more to maintain.
Option C (Process Builder field update, quick action, record type) — built on Process Builder, which Salesforce stopped supporting on 31 December 2025 and now points to Flow Builder to replace.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.lightning_app_builder_create_dynamic_action.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.lightning_page_components_visibility.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000389396&language=en_US&type=1

corrected.note: Key D stands, but the explanation led with the part of D that does not work. It opened by proposing separate Unqualified and Qualified record types with their own page layouts and relegated dynamic actions to a parenthesis; a page layout cannot vary with a picklist value, and no record type changes itself when Status changes. Create Dynamic Actions in Lightning App Builder documents the working mechanism in one line: "To add visibility rules based on the record field, device type, or other filters, click Add Filter." Also recorded for the deck's staleness sweep: option C is built on Process Builder, which reached end of support on 31 December 2025 - the key is unaffected, but the distractor now names a retired tool.

question: Universal Containers has several large customers that sell their products through dealers. Each customer and dealer has an individual rep who works directly with UC, and each is billed separately. How can an app builder implement these requirements?
optionA: Create a single account record, add each rep as a contact, and create a custom dealer object.
optionB: Create both customer and dealer as accounts, add each rep as a contact on the corresponding account, and create an account hierarchy.
optionC: Create a single parent record, add each rep as a contact to the parent account, and add each dealer as a child record.
optionD: Create both customer and dealer as accounts, create account teams on each account, and associate the dealer records with the parent account.
explanation:
Creating both customer and dealer as accounts, adding each rep as a contact on the corresponding account, and building an account hierarchy is how to implement it. Each entity that has its own bill and its own rep should be an Account; attaching each rep as a Contact on its account and using Parent Account to express the customer–dealer relationship is the standard pattern.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (one account, reps as contacts, a custom dealer object) — a dealer that is billed separately and has its own rep is an account, not a custom record hanging off someone else's.
Option C (one parent record, reps on the parent, dealers as child records) — puts every rep on the parent, losing who works with which dealer.
Option D (accounts with account teams, dealers associated to the parent) — account teams share access to one account; they do not model a dealer as a separate billed entity, and the option never says how the dealer is associated.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.account_parent_lex.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.account_hierarchy_setup_lex.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers implemented an application process that uses custom objects Internships and Applications. The organization-wide default for Internships has been set to private and is the master in the master-detail relationship with Applications. The VP of HR wants to allow edit access to Applications to recruiters. How should an app builder configure the proper access?
optionA: Set the organization-wide default on the Applications object to Read/Write.
optionB: Add a sharing rule that grants the users Read/Write access to the Internship records.
optionC: Create a queue for the web applications and assign access to the users who will be editing the records.
optionD: Create a sharing rule that grants the users Read/Write access to the Application records.
explanation:
Adding a sharing rule that grants the users Read/Write access to the Internship records is how to configure the access. Detail records inherit sharing from the master in a master-detail relationship — the detail object has no OWD or sharing rules of its own — so to give recruiters Read/Write on Applications, share the parent Internship records with them.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (OWD Read/Write on Applications) — a detail object in a master-detail relationship has no org-wide default to set; it is Controlled by Parent.
Option C (a queue for the applications) — queues take ownership of records; they do not grant edit access to a private master's details.
Option D (a sharing rule on Application records) — sharing rules cannot be defined on the detail side of a master-detail relationship.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.overview_of_custom_object_relationships.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An app builder wants to add the option to 'Send New Email' from Leads, Contacts, and Accounts for users on mobile. What is the benefit of using global actions to accomplish this?
optionA: Global actions can be accessed from many places — record pages, the publisher menu, feeds, and Chatter groups.
optionB: Salesforce Lightning Component Library houses existing global actions prebuilt for use.
optionC: The global action's layout automatically clones the default page layout.
optionD: Global actions are record-specific and are available when searching that particular object.
explanation:
Global actions being accessible from many places — record pages, the publisher menu, feeds and Chatter groups — is the benefit. Global actions are not tied to a specific object and can be surfaced in the global publisher, the Chatter feed, groups and the mobile navigation, letting users send a new email from Leads, Contacts or Accounts using the same action.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (prebuilt global actions in the Lightning Component Library) — the component library holds components, not global actions.
Option C (the layout clones the default page layout) — a global action has its own action layout, built separately.
Option D (record-specific, available when searching that object) — the opposite of a global action, which is by definition not tied to a record.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.actions_overview_global.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers uses the Asset object to track products that are installed at customer locations. A new object, Asset Inventory, has been created to capture details about the asset. Which approach should the app builder take to show Asset Inventory as a related list on Asset?
optionA: Create a roll-up on Asset. Add the Asset Inventory related list to the Asset page layout.
optionB: Create a junction object to relate Asset Inventory and Asset. Add the Asset Inventory related list to the Asset page layout.
optionC: Create a lookup relationship on Asset Inventory to Asset. Add the Asset Inventory related list to the Asset page layout.
optionD: Create a master-detail relationship on Asset to Asset Inventory. Add the Asset Inventory related list to the Asset page layout.
explanation:
Creating a lookup relationship on Asset Inventory to Asset, then adding the Asset Inventory related list to the Asset page layout, is the approach. A lookup (or master-detail) on the child object pointing to the parent is what produces a related list on the parent; a lookup is appropriate here unless cascade delete and inherited sharing are required, in which case master-detail would also work.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a roll-up on Asset) — a roll-up summarises related records; it creates no relationship and no related list.
Option B (a junction object) — models many-to-many; one asset's inventory details are one-to-many.
Option D (master-detail on Asset to Asset Inventory) — reversed: a master-detail must be created on the child object pointing to the parent.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.relationships_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.overview_of_custom_object_relationships.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Ursa Major Solar (UMS) uses a public sharing model for accounts. UMS would like to move to a more restrictive sharing model but wants the sales team to continue to have access to all account records with the sales record type. Which two actions should an app builder complete to implement this change? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Update the Sales profile.
optionC: Create a criteria-based sharing rule.
explanation:
Updating the organization-wide defaults, and creating a criteria-based sharing rule, are the two actions. First tighten the OWD on Account to Private (or Public Read Only); then create a criteria-based sharing rule that grants the sales team access to records where Record Type = Sales, restoring the access they need without opening up everything.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (update the Sales profile) — profiles set object permissions, not record-level sharing.
Option D (an owner-based sharing rule) — shares by who owns the record; the requirement is by record type, which is criteria.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.managing_the_sharing_model.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: When an opportunity Close Date is delayed by more than 60 days, the manager and the VP of Sales must approve the change. How can this requirement be met? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Build an approval process that requires unanimous approval from the manager and VP of Sales.
optionB: Create a workflow rule that checks for Close Date less than 60 days and add an email alert.
optionC: Create a record-triggered flow that submits the record for an approval process.
optionD: Build a validation rule that does not allow a user to save the opportunity record.
explanation:
An approval process requiring unanimous approval from the manager and VP of Sales, and a record-triggered flow that submits the record for approval, are the two answers. The requirement splits into two jobs: something has to collect the sign-offs, and something has to notice the change and start the process. In an approval step you choose Automatically assign to approver(s), name the manager and the VP of Sales, and select Require unanimous approval from all selected approvers, which Salesforce defines as approving the record only if everyone approves. Submit for Approval is a core action available to a flow, so a record-triggered flow on Opportunity whose entry conditions detect Close Date moving out by more than 60 days can submit the record automatically. Build this in Flow Builder: Salesforce ended support for Process Builder and Workflow Rules on 31 December 2025.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a workflow rule on Close Date less than 60 days with an email alert) — fails on every count: the criterion is inverted, it tests Close Date rather than the size of the delay, an email alert records no approval, and workflow is past end of support.
Option D (a validation rule blocking the save) — blocks the change outright, which is not what was asked: the delay is allowed, it just needs approval.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.approvals_step_approver.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_ref_elements_actions_approval.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000389396&language=en_US&type=1

corrected.note: Key A,C stands. The explanation offered Process Builder as an equal alternative to a record-triggered flow, which is now wrong guidance: support for Process Builder ended 31 December 2025 and Salesforce directs new automation to Flow Builder. The unanimous half is settled verbatim by the approval-step article: 'Require unanimous approval from all selected approvers. The record is approved only if everyone approves the request. If any approvers reject the request, the approval request is rejected.' Worth knowing for the rest of the deck's approval items: Salesforce has renamed this feature Classic Approval Processes and now promotes Flow Approval Processes as the modern alternative.

question: DreamHouse Realty is rethinking its sandbox utilization strategy after acquiring Cloud Kicks. The Salesforce CoE already utilizes a partial and a full sandbox, which they refresh on their own regular schedules. Teams are expanding and have to begin each of their small projects in a sandbox before committing to the larger pool for collaborative testing while still keeping costs down. What type of sandbox should each team member use?
optionA: Full sandbox
optionC: Developer Pro sandbox
explanation:
A Developer sandbox is the right size and, in this org, the right price. Sandbox Licenses and Storage Limits by Type gives it a 1-day refresh interval and 200 MB of data storage, copying metadata only — enough for one person's small project, and refreshable as often as that project needs. The cost argument is what rules out the nearest rival: Developer sandboxes come bundled with the add-ons the CoE has already bought — the Partial Copy add-on bundles 10 and the Full add-on bundles 15 — so DreamHouse already owns 25 at no extra cost.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Full sandbox) — the shared pool the question describes teams promoting into, with a 29-day refresh; unsuitable as personal scratch space even if the licences existed.
Option C (Developer Pro sandbox) — has to be purchased on top, and its extra 1 GB of storage buys nothing for a metadata-only project.
Option D (Partial sandbox) — the other half of the shared pool, with a 5-day refresh and a paid licence.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_environments.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Cloud Kicks wants to start tracking how many shoe subscriptions have been sold for each shoe catalog. A master-detail relationship exists between the Subscription__c and the Shoe__c objects. Which type of field should an app builder create?
optionA: Roll-up summary field
optionC: Master-detail relationship field
explanation:
A Roll-up summary field is the field type to create. With a master-detail relationship in place, a roll-up summary of type COUNT on the parent Shoe__c counting Subscription__c records gives an automatic, always-current subscription count.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Lookup field) — a relationship, not a count.
Option C (Master-detail relationship field) — already exists; a second one would not count anything.
Option D (Number field) — would have to be maintained by automation; a roll-up does it natively.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.fields_about_roll_up_summary_fields.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.overview_of_custom_object_relationships.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: What should an app builder consider when choosing a template for a new Lightning record page?
optionA: The template cannot be changed after the initial save.
optionB: To view the record page, users need View All Data permissions for the object.
optionC: The page structure will automatically adapt to the device being used to view the record page.
optionD: Select a new template for each type of device users use to view the record page.
explanation:
The page structure automatically adapting to the device being used is the consideration. The template you pick is what governs how the page appears across devices, not a separate page per device: standard record page templates support both desktop and phone, and in Lightning App Builder you use the form factor switcher to preview the page on each device the template supports. Device coverage is worth thinking about up front, because home page templates are desktop-only, and record page templates with pinned regions are desktop-only too — choosing one of those closes off the phone.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (the template cannot be changed after saving) — false; you can switch to a different template, subject to two documented rules: not to one supporting a narrower set of devices, and any component whose form factor the new template does not support is dropped at run time.
Option B (users need View All Data) — false; viewing a record page needs access to the record, not View All Data.
Option D (a new template per device) — you do not select a template per device; one template serves the form factors it supports.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.lightning_page_templates.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.lightning_app_builder_mobile_guidance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Key C stands as the only option that survives, but the explanation overstated it. It said Lightning page templates 'are responsive: their regions reflow for desktop, tablet, and phone form factors automatically', which the documentation contradicts: 'Home page templates are desktop-only. Standard app page templates support both desktop and phone. Standard record page templates support both desktop and phone, except the pinned region templates, which are desktop only. If a form factor isn't on the options list when you try to assign a Lightning page, then the page template doesn't support it.' The defensible version of C is the one the mobile-guidance article states - 'the template you choose controls how it appears across devices' - which is a reason to choose carefully, not a guarantee of automatic adaptation. The rewrite also nails down why A is false, since the same article documents the rules for switching a record page to a different template.

question: An app builder wants to use Process Builder to automate some of the work being done by the sales team. What are three capabilities of Process Builder that can improve productivity? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Send an email alert.
optionC: Send an outbound message.
explanation:
Sending an email alert, updating a related record, and creating a child record are the three Process Builder capabilities. Salesforce's own list of process actions settles this: create a record, invoke another process, create a Chatter post, use a quick action, work with Quip, launch a flow, send an email, send a custom notification, send a survey invitation, submit a record for approval, update records, and call Apex code.
Build this in Flow Builder rather than Process Builder. Support and updates for Process Builder ended on 31 December 2025; existing processes keep running but bugs are no longer fixed, and Salesforce provides a Migrate to Flow tool. Flow covers every capability listed above and adds the delete that Process Builder never had, through its Delete Records element.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (send an outbound message) — absent from the documented list; outbound messages were a Workflow Rule action, never a Process Builder one.
Option D (delete a related record) — there is no delete action in Process Builder.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.process_action.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000389396&language=en_US&type=1

corrected.note: Key A,B,E confirmed against the documented action list on Add Actions to Your Process, which contains no delete action and no outbound message action. The explanation was rewritten because it described Process Builder purely in the present tense as the tool to reach for. The same help page now carries the notice: 'Support and updates for Process Builder have ended as of December 31, 2025... For new automations, create flows in Flow Builder.' The key is unaffected - the item is a fair test of what Process Builder could do - but a learner should not leave it planning to build one.

question: Universal Containers uses a private sharing model on Accounts. User A and User B both own Accounts of their own and have both been sent a new account record in an email owned by User C to take a look at. User A is able to open and view the record but User B receives an insufficient privileges error. User A and User B have the same role in the role hierarchy. What are three reasons User A has access but User B is unable to access the record? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: User A is on the same account team as User C.
optionB: User A and User B have different profiles.
optionC: User C has manually shared the record with User A.
optionD: User A was granted an additional permission set.
optionE: User A is in a public group that has access via a sharing rule.
explanation:
User A being on the same account team as User C, User C having manually shared the record with User A, and User A being in a public group that has access via a sharing rule are the three reasons. With a private sharing model, access to one specific account has to come from a record-sharing mechanism, and all three are documented ways to give one user access without giving it to a peer in the same role. Salesforce lists the Account Team Member record alongside org-wide defaults, the role hierarchy, sharing rules and manual sharing as one of the methods that determine a user's access to an account; manual sharing exists for exactly this case, the owner opening up a single record to a specific coworker; and a criteria- or owner-based sharing rule targeting a public group reaches User A if they are in the group and not User B.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (different profiles) — weaker, but not for the reason usually given: profiles can reach record access through View All Records or Modify All Records, which ignore sharing, but that would open every account in the org, a much bigger change than the scenario describes, and the option does not say such a permission is present.
Option D (an additional permission set) — the same: a permission set could carry View All, but that cannot single out one account.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.accountteam_def.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.granting_access_to_records_lex.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_profiles_view_all_mod_all.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Key A,C,E stands, but the explanation's justification was documented-wrong. It claimed 'Profiles and permission sets control object/system permissions, not record-level access.' Considerations for Using Account Teams lists Profiles first among the access methods that 'determine users' access levels for accounts and related records', and the View All / Modify All article states that those permissions 'ignore sharing rules and settings, allowing administrators to grant access to records associated with a given object across the organization.' So the correct reason to reject B and D is granularity, not category: a permission set can grant account access, but only to every account at once, which doesn't match a scenario about one record.

question: Cloud Kicks has a sales rep who is stating that their Contact is unavailable for other users to see within Salesforce. In which three ways can an app builder troubleshoot this issue? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Create an Account sharing rule to give the users access to all records.
optionB: Confirm whether default organization-wide sharing settings provide access to the Account.
optionC: Review the Contact record and ensure it is linked to an Account.
optionD: Verify the users with the issue have access to the Contact object.
optionE: Create a new Contact and have the users try again.
explanation:
Confirming whether the org-wide sharing defaults provide access to the Account, reviewing whether the Contact is linked to an Account, and verifying the users have access to the Contact object are the three troubleshooting steps. Contact visibility is governed by the OWD and sharing model on the parent Account, by whether the Contact has a parent Account at all (private contacts are visible only to their owner), and by whether the affected users actually have Read on the Contact object through profile or permission set.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (an Account sharing rule giving everyone all records) — a change, not a diagnosis, and it opens far more than the one contact in question.
Option E (create a new Contact and try again) — reproduces nothing and explains nothing.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.contacts_sharing_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Sales reps at Universal Containers use Salesforce on their mobile devices. They want a way to add new contacts quickly and then follow up later to complete the additional information necessary. What mobile solution should an app builder recommend?
optionA: Customize the mobile menu to move Contacts to the top.
optionB: Build a global action to create Contacts.
optionC: Add a compact layout to Contacts.
optionD: Use Path and set predefined values.
explanation:
Building a global action to create Contacts is the mobile solution to recommend. A global Create-Contact quick action with only the essential fields on its action layout lets sales reps create a Contact from anywhere in the mobile app in a few taps, then return later to fill in the rest.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (move Contacts to the top of the mobile menu) — shortens the path to the list, not the form.
Option C (a compact layout on Contacts) — controls the fields shown in the record highlights, not what is captured on create.
Option D (Path with predefined values) — Path guides a picklist-driven process; it does not create records.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.actions_overview_global.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.predefined_field_values.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: At Ursa Solar Major, only users with the Outer Planets profile need to see the Jupiter field on the Solar System object. How should the app builder satisfy this requirement?
optionA: Classic encryption
optionC: Field-level security
explanation:
Field-level security is how the app builder satisfies the requirement. Field-level security controls which profiles and permission sets can see and edit a given field; hiding the Jupiter field for every profile except Outer Planets meets it exactly.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Classic encryption) — masks a field's value; it does not remove the field from other profiles' view.
Option B (filtered view) — not a Salesforce field-visibility feature.
Option D (sharing rules) — control record-level access, not field-level visibility.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_profiles_field_perms.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.managing_the_sharing_model.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers wants sales reps to get permission from their managers before deleting Opportunities. What can be used to meet these requirements?
optionA: Process Builder with Submit for Approval action.
optionB: Approval process with a triggered flow process.
optionC: Approval process with time-dependent workflow action.
explanation:
An approval process with a triggered flow process is what can meet the requirement. Deletion cannot be gated by an approval process on its own: a classic approval process supports exactly four automated actions — Task, Email Alert, Field Update, Outbound Message — so it can route the decision and record the outcome, but it can neither delete the opportunity nor stop a rep deleting it while the request is pending. That makes this a two-part build: a record-triggered flow submits the opportunity for approval automatically, and a second record-triggered flow configured to run before the record is deleted blocks the deletion with a Custom Error element until the approval has come back. Salesforce documents that element for exactly this: "when a user deletes a record that triggers a flow, the flow can return an error message that tells the user why the deletion was not allowed."
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Process Builder with Submit for Approval) — fails on a hard limitation: Process Builder's Record Change trigger offers only "only when a record is created" and "when a record is created or edited", so a process cannot run on a delete at all and can never enforce the gate. Salesforce also ended support for Process Builder on 31 December 2025.
Option C (approval process with a time-dependent workflow action) — schedules something for later rather than blocking anything, and rests on Workflow Rules, retired on the same date.
Option D (two-step approval process) — adds a second approver to a problem whose difficulty was never the number of approvers.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.approvals_automated_actions.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.process_start.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_ref_elements_custom_error.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000389396&language=en_US&type=1

corrected.note: Answer moved A to B. The earlier pass kept A on the reasoning that a process genuinely can submit for approval and that the exam key should stand; further checking shows the item is decided by a capability limit, not by tool preference. Process Builder Record Change trigger offers only "only when a record is created" and "when a record is created or edited", and its remaining trigger types are Event and Invocable - so a process cannot run on a delete under any configuration, and option A cannot enforce a gate on deletion however it is built. A record-triggered flow can: it runs on delete and blocks one with a Custom Error element, which uses the same functionality as the addError() method in Apex. The approval process itself deletes nothing either way - Add Automated Actions to a Classic Approval Process lists four action types (Task, Email Alert, Field Update, Outbound Message) and none is a delete. That also disposes of the duplication that made this item ambiguous: A and B are no longer the same design in two tools, because only one of the two tools can reach a delete.

question: An app builder is preparing to deploy a new app from the sandbox to production using change sets. What two considerations should an app builder keep in mind during this process? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Salesforce Connect automatically establishes a link between environments.
optionB: Change sets do not include all components and may have to perform some changes manually.
optionC: All users must be logged out of the target org before a change set can be deployed.
optionD: Transactions will revert if the deployment errors.
explanation:
Change sets not including every component, so some changes must be made manually, and the deployment transaction reverting on error, are the two considerations. A change set carries only the metadata types it supports, so parts of an app routinely have to be reconfigured by hand in the target org after the deployment lands. And Salesforce is explicit: "A change set is deployed in a single transaction. If the deployment is unable to complete for any reason, the entire transaction is rolled back." The symmetrical half is worth remembering — once a deployment succeeds, all changes are committed and it cannot be rolled back.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Salesforce Connect links the environments) — false in a way that is easy to miss: Salesforce Connect surfaces external data as external objects; it moves no metadata. What connects two orgs for change sets is a deployment connection, which exists automatically between a production org and its sandboxes and must be authorised to receive inbound changes.
Option C (all users must be logged out) — false; Salesforce documents no user-session precondition, and change sets are routinely deployed into live production orgs. The only in-flight work it asks you to think about is Apex, through a Deployment Settings option about pending Apex jobs.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.changesets_inbound_deploy.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.changesets_about_connection.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.changesets_about_components.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note:
Key B,D confirmed. This item previously had a defective option set: its original option C read "A deployment connection between source and target orgs must be authorized before change sets can be sent", which Deployment Connections for Change Sets states almost verbatim — giving the question three true options in a "choose 2". Option C has been replaced with a false statement in the same subject area (that all users must be logged out before a deployment), so the item now has exactly two correct answers. Treat the new option C as authored, not original.

Superseded note from the 2026-08-11 pass, kept because its citations still stand: DEFECTIVE ITEM - flagged to the user. Key B,D preserved, but this 'choose 2' has three true options. C is documented almost word for word by Deployment Connections for Change Sets: 'A deployment connection alone doesn't enable change sets to be sent between orgs. Each org must be authorized to send and receive change sets. This added level of security enforces code promotion paths.' Only A is false. The explanation now says so explicitly rather than leaving a learner who picked C thinking they misunderstood the platform. D itself is settled by Deploy a Change Set: 'A change set is deployed in a single transaction. If the deployment is unable to complete for any reason, the entire transaction is rolled back.'

question: An app builder at Cloud Kicks created a custom object and related fields in the Schema Builder. What next steps should the app builder take to ensure users can access the new object and fields?
optionA: Create a permission set for access to the object and fields.
optionB: Allow reporting for the object and fields.
optionC: Assign data types to the fields on the object.
optionD: Add the fields to the page layout on the object.
explanation:
Creating a permission set for access to the object and fields is the next step. Schema Builder creates the metadata, but newly created custom objects and fields are not automatically visible to non-admin users; the app builder must grant object and field permissions through a profile or, preferably, a permission set.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (allow reporting) — a checkbox that makes the object reportable; it grants no user access.
Option C (assign data types) — fields cannot be created without a data type; that step is already done.
Option D (add the fields to the page layout) — necessary for display, but useless until users have object and field permissions.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.perm_set_groups.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_profiles_field_perms.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An app builder has downloaded a component from the AppExchange successfully; however, they are unable to add it to the Lightning home page. Which two reasons can be preventing the app builder from being able to add the custom component? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: My Domain must be deployed to add custom components to the page with the App Builder.
optionB: A custom tab must be created to add custom components to the page with the App Builder.
optionC: The component requires a developer permission to add it to the page with the App Builder.
optionD: The component is tagged for record pages instead of home pages and is not showing up in the App Builder.
explanation:
My Domain needing to be deployed, and the component being tagged for record pages instead of home pages, are the two keyed reasons. The component's target is the live cause: a Lightning component declares where it can be used through the targets in its configuration file, and a component that declares only lightning__RecordPage simply does not appear in the palette when you are editing a Home page — nothing is broken, the component is telling App Builder it is not a Home page component.
The My Domain answer is historical and worth understanding rather than memorising. Custom Lightning components have always required My Domain, but that prerequisite can no longer be the blocker: Salesforce now states that all orgs get a My Domain with enhanced domains by default, so there is no longer an org in which My Domain is undeployed and waiting to be turned on.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a custom tab must be created) — a custom tab is one way to expose an app or object, not a precondition for placing a component on a page.
Option C (a developer permission is required) — no such permission gates the App Builder palette; creating and saving Lightning pages needs Customize Application, which the app builder already has.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/targets-lightning-utility-bar.html
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.domain_name_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.lightning_app_builder_create_dynamic_action.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Key A,D kept, with a staleness flag on A. The My Domain overview now states 'All orgs get a My Domain with enhanced domains by default', so option A describes a prerequisite that is satisfied everywhere and can no longer explain a component missing from the palette. D remains a live, everyday cause - a component's targets decide which page types it appears on. The key is unchanged because A is still the documented requirement and there is no better third option (B and C are both false), but the explanation now dates A rather than presenting it as something to go and check.

question: Cloud Kicks (CK) wants to quickly insert a list of over 60,000 net-new Accounts. The template based on CK's data model was used to populate the list. Which tool should be used?
optionA: Data Loader
optionC: Import Wizard
explanation:
Data Loader is the tool. The record count decides it: Salesforce's guidance is to use the Data Import Wizard when 'you're loading less than 50,000 records', and 60,000 net-new Accounts is over that line in a single load. Data Loader handles CSV files of up to 150 million records, and Account is a supported object. The guidance lists other reasons to reach for Data Loader that also fit: objects the wizard does not support, complex field mappings applied consistently, scheduled or repeated loads, and exports for backup.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Lightning Object Creator) — builds a new custom object from a spreadsheet, but Account already exists and CK's template is built on its existing data model.
Option C (Import Wizard) — capped at 50,000 records per load.
Option D (Schema Builder) — designs schema and loads no data at all.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.dataLoader.meta/dataLoader/when_to_use_the_data_loader.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.faq_data_import_wizard_what_kind_objects.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Key A stands; the explanation carried a stale number. It said 'Data Loader handles up to 5 million records per load via Bulk API'. The current Data Loader Guide says 150 million: 'Data loader supports CSV files with a maximum 150,000,000 records. If you must load more than 150 million records, we recommend you work with a Salesforce partner or visit the AppExchange for a suitable partner product.' The 50,000 ceiling on the Data Import Wizard is confirmed by the same page - 'Use Data Import Wizard When: You're loading less than 50,000 records' - and is the fact the item actually turns on.

question: Universal Containers asked the app builder to ensure when an Account Type changes to 'Past-Customer' the Contacts directly related to that Account get an updated status of 'Re-Market'. Which automation should the app builder use to accomplish this task?
optionA: Screen flow
optionC: Validation rule
explanation:
A record-triggered flow is the automation to use. A record-triggered flow on Account fires on the change itself, with entry conditions set so it runs only when Type becomes Past-Customer, and it can then write to records other than the one that triggered it. Build the update as a single Update Records element rather than a loop: choosing 'specify conditions to identify records and set fields individually' lets one element filter for the Contacts whose AccountId matches the triggering account and set Status to Re-Market on all of them at once.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (screen flow) — needs a user to run it, which defeats an automation meant to fire on a field change.
Option B (Lightning component) — custom development for a declarative problem.
Option C (validation rule) — can only block a save; it cannot write a value to a related record.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_build_data_update.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.flow_considerations_trigger_record.htm&type=5

corrected.note: Key D stands; the explanation prescribed the wrong flow shape. It said the flow should 'loop through related Contacts and update each one's status', which is the pattern Salesforce's own guidance avoids. Update Salesforce Records from a Flow documents the one-element alternative: 'Update Records, where you chose to specify conditions and set fields individually - In the same element, use filter criteria', updating 'at least one' record, and notes that 'Quick Action elements can update only one record at a time, while Update Records elements can update multiple records.' Same answer, but the rewritten prose teaches bulk-safe flow design instead of per-record DML.

question: The VP of Sales at Universal Containers has asked the app builder to let sales reps create opportunity records directly from the Account, with a number of fields pre-populated. Which feature should the app builder use to allow users to create the opportunity?
optionA: A quick action
optionC: A custom button
explanation:
A quick action is the feature. An object-specific Create Opportunity quick action on Account lets you define a tailored action layout and predefined field values, so reps can create the related Opportunity from the Account with the right fields prefilled.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a default action) — not a Salesforce feature name; the standard New button carries no predefined values.
Option C (a custom button) — could open a URL with parameters, but prefilling by URL is unsupported in Lightning where a quick action's predefined values are the documented mechanism.
Option D (a custom link) — the same limitation as a custom button, without even a button placement.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.predefined_field_values.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.actions_in_lex.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: When a deal is Closed Won, it has to be approved by the owner's manager prior to being added to the leaderboard for a quarterly sales competition. An opportunity is won on the last day of the quarter and the manager is on vacation. What is recommended to ensure all of the appropriate deals are reviewed and the leaderboard is up to date?
optionA: Forward the approval request to the manager's assistant.
optionB: Set up a delegated approver for the manager.
optionC: Have the manager log on and reassign the approval request.
optionD: Use Process Builder to assign a delegated approver.
explanation:
Setting up a delegated approver for the manager is the recommendation. Each user record has a Delegated Approver field; configuring one for the vacationing manager allows the delegate to approve incoming requests on the manager's behalf — the standard solution for out-of-office approval coverage.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (forward the request to the assistant) — approval requests cannot be forwarded to someone who is not an approver or delegate.
Option C (have the manager log on and reassign) — defeats the point of the manager being on vacation, and the deals need to be reviewed on the last day.
Option D (Process Builder to assign a delegated approver) — the delegated approver is a user setting, not something a process assigns; and Process Builder is past end of support.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.approvals_change_approval_user_pref.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.approvals_step_approver.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has 20 different workflows on the Opportunity object. To ensure that updates are processing properly for all field updates, UC has the 'Re-evaluate workflow rules after field change' checkbox checked. Recently after adding a new workflow, users have reported receiving errors about workflow limits. What should an app builder look at to address this?
optionA: Talk to a developer about Apex code issues.
optionB: Number of workflows per object limits.
optionC: Workflows that cause each other to fire back and forth recursively.
optionD: Workflows on other objects that are being re-triggered.
explanation:
Workflows that cause each other to fire back and forth recursively are what the app builder should look at. With Re-evaluate Workflow Rules After Field Change turned on, a field update that changes a value causes Salesforce to reevaluate every workflow rule on that object, and any rule newly meeting its criteria fires; if one of those performs another reevaluating field update, the cascade continues — up to five times after the initial update. Salesforce names the failure mode directly: if a field update for Rule1 triggers Rule2 and a field update for Rule2 triggers Rule1, the recursive triggers can push the org past its limit of 1,000 workflow time triggers per hour. The newly added rule is what closed the loop.
Note that Workflow Rules reached end of support on 31 December 2025. Existing rules keep running, but the fix here is to migrate this automation to Flow Builder, where a single record-triggered flow replaces rules that were reevaluating each other.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Apex code issues) — misdirects to Apex in an org where the symptom is a documented workflow behaviour.
Option B (workflows-per-object limits) — checkable and wrong: the limits are 50 active and 500 total rules per object, and UC has 20.
Option D (workflows on other objects being re-triggered) — ruled out by the mechanism: only rules on the same object as the initial field update are reevaluated, and cross-object rules are not candidates for reevaluation at all.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.workflow_field_updates_reevalute_wf.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.workflow_limits.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000389396&language=en_US&type=1

corrected.note: Key C stands, with the mechanism made precise and two distractors now disposed of by documented facts rather than by plausibility. Field Updates That Reevaluate Workflow Rules: 'This cascade of workflow rule reevaluation and triggering can happen up to five times after the initial field update that started it', and the recursive Rule1/Rule2 example ends 'can cause your organization to exceed its limit for workflow time triggers per hour' - which Workflow Limits puts at 1,000 per hour. The same page kills D: 'Only workflow rules on the same object as the initial field update are reevaluated and triggered... Cross-object workflow rules aren't candidates for reevaluation.' And B fails on the published numbers, 50 active and 500 total rules per object against UC's 20. The original explanation's vague 'recursion/governor limits' has been replaced with those figures, and the Workflow Rules end-of-support date added.

question: DreamHouse Realty (DR) employees started using company-owned airplanes for work travel after Ursa Major Solar was acquired.
